questions.q: What is migration script 0047_AddHazmatFlagToLoads.sql, and why does it matter that it exists as a numbered file in a repository rather than as text typed into an SSMS query window?
options: It's a version-controlled record of one discrete schema change, so what changed, when, and why is preserved instead of being lost the way prior changes always were on DispatchDB
It's a backup of the entire Loads table, unrelated to schema changes
It's a SQL Server system file automatically generated whenever ALTER TABLE runs
It only matters for auditing purposes and has no effect on how the change is actually deployed
questions.explain: Chapter 9's version control practice means every schema change is a saved, numbered script in source control — exactly what was missing on MERSQL01 before this capstone, where changes vanished the moment they were typed.

questions.q: Why is the rollback script for migration 0047 written and reviewed before the forward script is ever run against production?
options: Because writing it under pressure after a failed deployment is riskier and more error-prone than preparing and reviewing it calmly ahead of time
SQL Server requires a rollback script to exist before ALTER TABLE will execute
It has no real benefit; it's written first purely as a documentation formality
Because rollback scripts cannot be written after a column has already been added
questions.explain: Rollback planning ahead of time (per Chapter 9 and Chapter 11's rollback planning lesson) avoids improvising a reversal under pressure during an incident, when mistakes are more likely.

questions.q: Why does the migration get tested against a restored copy of DispatchDB on a staging instance before going to production?
options: To confirm the script runs cleanly and the application's new behavior works correctly, without any risk to the live production database
Staging testing is required by SQL Server before any ALTER TABLE statement can run in production
It replaces the need for a pull request review
It has no real value since the script was already reviewed
questions.explain: Testing on a restored copy validates both the script's correctness and the application's behavior against the new schema, catching problems before they can affect real dispatch operations.

questions.q: Why is the actual deployment of migration 0047 wrapped in an explicit BEGIN TRANSACTION / COMMIT TRANSACTION?
options: So that if any statement in the script fails partway through, the whole change can be rolled back cleanly instead of leaving DispatchDB in a half-changed state
Because ALTER TABLE statements cannot run without an explicit transaction
To make the deployment run faster
Because CREATE INDEX requires a transaction wrapper to complete
questions.explain: Wrapping a multi-statement deployment in a transaction ensures atomicity — either every statement succeeds together, or none of them take effect, avoiding a partially applied schema change.

questions.q: After deployment, what does the lesson do to make sure the next person who inherits DispatchDB doesn't face the same undocumented-schema problem the capstone started with?
options: Records the deployment — script number, date, reviewer, and who ran it — in a change log that didn't previously exist
Deletes the migration script once it has been applied, since it's no longer needed
Relies on sys.columns alone as the permanent record of what changed
Nothing further is done once the deployment succeeds
questions.explain: The change log entry — capturing what changed, when, and by whom — is exactly the documentation that was missing when this capstone began, closing the gap identified in Lesson 64.
